newsitem.title: PERU: Peru poll says Fujimori's popularity rises - report.
newsitem.headline: Peru poll says Fujimori's popularity rises - report.

text.p: A peruvian pollster said Friday the popularity of President Alberto Fujimori has increased during the ongoing hostage crisis, local television reported.
Fujimori's approval rating rose to 50.3 percent in January from 44.9 percent in December according to pollster, Compania Peruana de Investigacion de Mercados (CPI).

In the first survey published since Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels took over the Japanese ambassador's residence, disapproval of Fujimori was virtually unchanged, slipping to 44.5 percent from 44.9 percent a month ago.
The improvement in his approval rating came from increased support form those who previously held no opinion, the televison report said, without giving details of the number of people polled.

While many Peruvians have seen much truth in the MRTA's complaints about poverty in Peru, there has been general disgust at their methods and strong support for what Fujimori calls his "firm but prudent" approach to the crsis.
The poll said 65.9 percent believed Fujimori's handling of the crisis was correct, while 23.1 percent disagreed and 11.0 percent held no opinion.

Fujimori has said he will look for a peaceful solution to the 31-day siege. He has rejected the rebels' main demand for the relaese of some 400 jailed comrades and said he will not rule out using force until the hostage takers lay down their arms and free all 74 of their captives.
The poll said an overwhelming 93.2 percent of the population believed the president should look for a peaceful solution to the siege and 88.2 percent said no rebels should be released from prison.
Since taking office in 1990, the president had held high popularity ratings due to the virtual defeat of communist guerrillas, economic reforms and a strong, personalized leadership style.
But Fujimori had held high popularity ratings during most of his time in office due to the virtual defeat of communist guerrillas, economic reforms and a strong, personalized leadership style.
But last year his popularity plummeted to its lowest level in five years.

The administration's failure to reduce high levels of poverty and unemployment, Fujimori's perceived authoritarianism, and his possible bid for a third term, took a a toll on his popularity, analysts say.

Fujimori could run for an unprecedented third term in 2000, if he wanted, according to a Constitutional Court ruling Thursday. The court decided a bid to stop Fujimori standing again on legal grounds was "unfounded."
